title: Foundations of Agentic AI Patterns
subtitle: Knowledge Check
intro: Check your understanding of Module 1: Foundations of Agentic AI Patterns. Pick an answer for each question and submit. Correct answers are confirmed; for a wrong answer you get a hint (the right answer is not revealed) and you try again until you get it right.

questions.prompt: A development team is building an AI solution that must make autonomous decisions, adapt to changing conditions, and work toward objectives without constant human intervention. Which key characteristic indicates that an agentic AI solution is required?
options: The need for a large language model with a broad knowledge base.
The requirement for cyclical decision-making with continuous adaptation.
The desire for faster response times and improved performance.
The preference for cloud-based deployment over on-premises solutions.
questions.answer: The requirement for cyclical decision-making with continuous adaptation.
questions.why: The correct answer is B, the requirement for cyclical decision-making with continuous adaptation. Let's review why. Option A, the need for a large language model, is incorrect, because the mere presence of an LLM does not make a system agentic; traditional applications use LLMs too. Option B is correct, because agentic AI is defined by its cyclical, adaptive decision-making, where the agent keeps working with its components until it gets the result right. That continuous adaptation and autonomy is exactly what sets it apart from a linear input-to-output system. Option C, faster response times, is incorrect, because performance improvements are not unique to agentic AI. And option D, cloud versus on-premises deployment, is incorrect, because deployment location is not a defining characteristic; both traditional and agentic AI run in many environments.

questions.prompt: Which five components form the essential architecture of an agentic system?
options: Runtime, Policy, Browser, Code Interpreter, and Identity.
Framework or agent code, Memory, Tools, LLM, and Inter-agent communication.
Observability, Security, Deployment Monitoring, and Evaluation.
Short-term memory, Long-term memory, Semantic memory, Episodic memory, and Working memory.
questions.answer: Framework or agent code, Memory, Tools, LLM, and Inter-agent communication.
questions.why: The correct answer is B: framework or agent code, memory, tools, the large language model, and inter-agent communication. Let's review the others. Option A lists Runtime, Policy, Browser, Code Interpreter, and Identity; these are AgentCore services, not the essential architectural components of an agent. Option C lists observability, security, deployment monitoring, and evaluation; these are important considerations you must manage, but they are not the core building blocks. And option D lists several memory types; memory is critical, but it is just one of the five components, not the whole architecture. Option B is correct because it captures the five essential elements: the framework and code for orchestration, the LLM for reasoning, memory for context, tools for taking action, and inter-agent communication for collaboration.

questions.prompt: A team already has several existing REST APIs and Lambda functions, and they want their agent to call them as tools without writing custom integration code for each one. Which AgentCore service is designed to address this need?
options: AgentCore Runtime, because it is the execution environment that hosts and scales the agent.
AgentCore Memory, because it manages the context the agent needs to call external systems.
AgentCore Gateway, which simplifies tool discovery and integration by transforming existing APIs, Lambda functions, and services into agent-compatible tools.
AgentCore Observability, because it monitors and traces every tool invocation the agent makes.
questions.answer: AgentCore Gateway, which simplifies tool discovery and integration by transforming existing APIs, Lambda functions, and services into agent-compatible tools.
questions.why: The correct answer is C, AgentCore Gateway, which simplifies tool discovery and integration by transforming existing APIs, Lambda functions, and services into agent-compatible tools. Let's review why. Option A, AgentCore Runtime, is incorrect, because Runtime is the execution environment that hosts and scales the agent; it does not turn existing APIs into callable tools. Option B, AgentCore Memory, is incorrect, because Memory handles context management, both short-term and long-term, and has nothing to do with tool integration. Option C is correct, because Gateway is purpose-built for exactly this: it takes your existing REST APIs, Lambda functions, and services and exposes them as tools the agent can discover and call, which removes the need to hand-write a custom integration for each one. Option D, AgentCore Observability, is incorrect, because Observability provides monitoring and tracing of agent behavior; it can see tool calls but does not create the tool integrations in the first place.

questions.prompt: A team has a compelling agent demo but keeps struggling to deploy that same agent reliably at scale in production. In the context of this module, what is the "prototype-to-production chasm," and how does AgentCore relate to it?
options: The chasm is the gap between a working proof of concept and an enterprise-ready deployment, defined by hard problems like scalability, security, performance, and state management, and AgentCore was purpose-built to bridge it.
The chasm is the difficulty of choosing which foundation model to use, and AgentCore resolves it by selecting the model for you.
The chasm is the cost of training a model on GPUs, and AgentCore bridges it by making training cheaper.
The chasm is the incompatibility between two agent frameworks, and AgentCore bridges it by forcing every agent onto a single required framework.
questions.answer: The chasm is the gap between a working proof of concept and an enterprise-ready deployment, defined by hard problems like scalability, security, performance, and state management, and AgentCore was purpose-built to bridge it.
questions.why: The correct answer is A: the chasm is the gap between a working proof of concept and an enterprise-ready deployment, defined by hard problems like scalability, security, performance, and state management, and AgentCore was purpose-built to bridge it. Let's review why. Option A is correct, because the module describes how it is relatively easy to get a basic agent working for a demo, but getting that same agent into production is where the real work begins, and that gap is defined by scalability, security, performance, and complex state management, which is precisely the gap AgentCore was built to close. Option B is incorrect, because the chasm is not about picking a foundation model; AgentCore is explicitly model-agnostic and works with any large language model. Option C is incorrect, because the module does not frame the chasm as GPU training cost; agents build on existing LLMs rather than training their own. Option D is incorrect, because AgentCore is framework-agnostic and works with any agent framework, so it does not force a single required framework.

questions.prompt: In AgentCore Identity, which statement correctly distinguishes inbound authentication from outbound authentication?
options: Inbound authentication establishes the agent's identity to reach external systems, while outbound authentication verifies the end user accessing the agent.
Both inbound and outbound authentication rely only on IAM and never integrate with external identity providers.
Outbound authentication is only about encrypting data at rest, while inbound authentication handles everything else.

Inbound authentication verifies who the user is and whether they may interact with the agent, while outbound authentication establishes the agent's own identity and its authorization to access external resources on the user's behalf.
questions.answer: Inbound authentication verifies who the user is and whether they may interact with the agent, while outbound authentication establishes the agent's own identity and its authorization to access external resources on the user's behalf.
questions.why: The correct answer is D: inbound authentication verifies who the user is and whether they may interact with the agent, while outbound authentication establishes the agent's own identity and its authorization to access external resources on the user's behalf. Let's review why. Option A is incorrect, because it reverses the two directions; inbound is about the user reaching the agent, not the agent reaching external systems. Option B is incorrect, because Identity integrates with your existing identity providers so you do not have to migrate users, so it is not limited to IAM. Option C is incorrect, because encrypting data at rest is not one of the two authentication directions at all; outbound authentication is about the agent proving its identity and authorization to external resources. Option D is correct, because it matches the module exactly: inbound authentication confirms the user and their permission to interact with the agent, and outbound authentication lets the agent establish its own identity and authorization to act on the user's behalf against external resources.
